FindName: First Jewish Revolt Year Five Silver Shekel
Description: A silver shekel of the First Jewish Revolt, about 13.25-13.9 g, dated Year 5 (April to August AD 70), with the same chalice and 'Shekel of Israel' obverse and pomegranates and 'Jerusalem the Holy' reverse as the earlier years. Year 5 shekels are the rarest of all First Revolt shekels - about 12 to 13 known from the classic die sets according to the Menorah Coin Project - struck in only about four months before Titus captured Jerusalem and destroyed the temple in the autumn of AD 70. Several Year 5 shekels were excavated at Masada, showing that some fighters escaped Jerusalem before it fell.
Interpretations: Meshorer noted the striking fact that silver shekels kept being minted in the last four months of the war even after bronze coinage stopped entirely, because paying the half-shekel temple tax remained all-important to the defenders. After the war the revolt coins were banned and many were melted for their silver, which helps explain their rarity. The Year 5 shekel is therefore evidence of worship continuing under siege, not of a functioning economy.
BiblicalSignificance: Exodus 30:13 is the tax these last shekels were struck to pay, and Matthew 24:2 records Jesus's prediction that not one stone of the temple would be left on another - the destruction that ended their minting within months.
CurrentLocation: Israel Museum, Jerusalem and other collections (examples)
